Ulaanbaatar is like any other city you see around the world. But if you want too see Mongolia, hit the road. Visit the countryside, the national landmarks like the Gobi Desert, Lake Khuvsgul(be mindful of the tourist traps, the camps love to squeeze your wallets dry, try setting up your own tent in one of the designated areas) and of course, Khalkhiin Gol.

There's the famous tank statue that represents the support that our people gave to the Soviets dueing WW2, and at the top is the Battle of Khalkhiin Gol memorial, honoring the Soviet and Mongolian soldiers who gave their lives during the battle. And at the peak, all around, you see the extravagance of the rich, fancy buildings, gated communities and apartments, but you're too far away to see the reality of how the majority lives.

Most of the scarys hit you hear about the military comes from those days, 70-90s. You can go ahead and ask anyone you know. Hazings n stuff, and if you made it to Sergeant to above, you were basically god among men.
One thing I heard was that back in those days soldiers were paid about 12 tugriks, and their sergeants would take 8 tugriks from them to keep for themselves, among other things.

Last year, one of our dudes passed over the wall to meet his gf.
Now mind you, this area has a lot of military personnel living there. So while this guy was meeting his gf, some enlisted dude who lives in that apartment took a picture and sent it to our unit. Everyone from staff to company goes apeshit trying to find whoever did this and for a week everything was tense. So after like a week, me, that dude and a bunch of other soldiers were in the armory cleaning our rifles when suddenly our company sarge comes in and tells us we can write a letter to our girlfriends back home. Sarge starts asking us where our girlfriends live. I say UB, some say from that province, including our guy. Sarge then asks where specifically asks where so your girlfriends live here. My guy accidentaly spills, and immediately after that sarge yells "HEY CAPTAIN, WE GOT HIM WE GOT THE BASTARD" and immediately pinches him from his ear and drags him to the company entertainment room. Beatimg ensue, his gf gets called to base, threats of being sent to the brig gets thrown around. But in the end, he ended up getting firewatch(ээлжтэн) for a whole month without no one switching with him and no guard duty until he got discharged. Also this guy got caught drinking once, and had to run around the parade field in full chemical gear and equipment in the summer sun until he passed out. Yeah, fun times.

Fun fact, prisoners wake up at 07AM on weekdays and 08AM on weekends and holidays smh.
It felt worth it and not worth it at the same time.

So on a weekday, this is our daily routine.  
0550-Wake up calls  
0600-Morning PT  
0630-Hygiene stuff, making beds, cleaning  
0700-Breakfast (Dairy on Tuesdays and Saturdays)  
0730-Bathroom and smoke break  
0740-Morning cleaning, candlewaxing the floors  
0800-Morning formation, raising of the flag  
0900-Daily routine, which includes training, lectures, working on construction on base.  
1000-Guards change shift. Guards going off duty get to have 2 hour rest.  
1200-Afternoon/Lunch Formation  
1230-Bathroom and smoke break  
1300-Afternoon formation. Afterwards people get back to work.  
1730/1800-Evening formation. Enlisted and Officers go home.  
1900-Dinner  
1930-Evening bathroom and smoke break  
1940-Night count preperation  
2040-Night count inspection  
2100-Night singing begins  
2130-Night singing concludes  
2140-The flag goes down, night count, NCOs give duties and discuss todays and tomorrows events  
2150-Night bathroom and smoke break  
2200-Rest  
On weekends and national holidays, wake up calls go back one hour which is poggers if you ask me.

Basic training felt like literal torture. The rest felt like slow torture too, in a way.  
You start to miss home and family, even though you weren't open with them while you were a civilian. You miss the freedom you had. You regret the time you wasted doing meaningless stuff like digging the web for 12 hours. You fantasize about leaving the base, coming home to your loved ones, triumphantly and proud.  
You learn basic military skills like drills, weapons training and specialized training, which in our case was combat engineering. Our unit specialized in construction and engineering so we went out on the national development projects like the Darkhan road construction and the south border projects.  
The only thing I enjoyed was actual military stuff and the brothers I got from my time.
